title: Implementing Interfaces
summary: Master the implements keyword: compiler contract enforcement, method overriding visibility rules, and combining class inheritance with interface implementation.
learningObjectives: Use the implements keyword to establish binding contracts between classes and interfaces
Identify compiler errors when visibility is reduced or methods are omitted
Combine class inheritance (extends) with interface adoption (implements) in a single class
Differentiate compile-time reference type constraints from runtime object capabilities
expectedOutcomes: You can implement complex interfaces with 100% compliance with access modifier rules
You can combine extends and implements cleanly in domain classes

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The FAA Commercial Pilot Certification

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: To fly a Boeing 787 for a commercial airline, a pilot must hold an FAA Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) license. The FAA does not care whether the pilot was born in California or France, or went to military flight school or a private aviation academy (their class ancestry). What matters is that the pilot passed every single requirement: instrument navigation, crosswind landing, and emergency de-pressurization.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: The FAA ATP license is the `interface` (`PilotLicense`). The individual pilot is a `Person` class that `implements PilotLicense`. If the pilot fulfills 9 out of 10 requirements, the FAA will NOT grant the license—every single check must pass.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Adopting an interface is an all-or-nothing legal contract: every method must be fully satisfied before the compiler permits the class to exist.

activities.title: Rules of Implementation & The extends + implements Syntax
Combining extends SuperClass implements Interface
activities.explanation: SeniorEngineer inherits state and methods from Employee (IS-A) while fulfilling the contract from BonusEligible (CAN-DO).

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `SeniorEngineer extends Employee implements BonusEligible` uses correct keyword ordering.
`calculateBonus` is implemented as `public` matching the interface requirement.
Caller accesses both inherited Employee methods and BonusEligible methods.

activities.title: Abstract Class Implementing an Interface
activities.explanation: BaseSqlRepository implements Repository but only implements delete(). Because BaseSqlRepository is abstract, this is 100% legal. UserRepository implements the rest.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `UserRepository` is concrete and provides the remaining implementations for `save` and `findById`.
`Repository repo = new UserRepository()` invokes all 3 methods seamlessly.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax order when a class extends a base class and implements an interface?
options: class C implements I extends B {}
class C extends B implements I {}
class C inherits B uses I {}
class C (B, I) {}
questions.explanation: Java syntax strictly mandates that `extends SuperClass` must precede `implements InterfaceName`.

questions.question: What error occurs if an implementing class method omits the `public` access modifier?
options: The method automatically becomes public with a compiler warning
Compilation error: cannot reduce the visibility of the inherited method from Interface
Runtime IllegalAccessException
The method is ignored by the interface
questions.explanation: Interface methods are implicitly public. Omitting `public` in the implementing class gives it package-private access, which narrows visibility and fails compilation.

questions.question: Can an abstract class implement an interface without providing implementations for any of its methods?
options: No, at least one method must be implemented
Yes, an abstract class is not obligated to implement interface methods; it passes that obligation to concrete subclasses
Only if the interface has no constants
Only in default package
questions.explanation: An abstract class can implement an interface and provide zero method bodies, delegating the entire implementation contract to concrete child classes.

questions.question: What happens if a concrete class implements an interface but omits one of the required methods?
options: The missing method generates a runtime error only when invoked
The compiler fails to compile the class: 'Class must either be declared abstract or implement abstract method'
The missing method is given a default null return
The interface is silently discarded
questions.explanation: Contract fulfillment is checked at compile time. Omitting any method from a concrete class halts compilation.

questions.question: Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
options: No, Java only allows single interface implementation
Yes, a class can implement multiple interfaces separated by commas: `class A implements I1, I2, I3`
Only if all interfaces have the same method names
Only in Java Enterprise Edition
questions.explanation: Java supports multiple interface inheritance: a single class can implement as many comma-separated interfaces as needed.

questions.question: Can an interface reference invoke methods that are declared in the implementing class but NOT in the interface?
options: Yes, because the actual object has those methods
No, the compiler restricts callable methods to those declared on the reference type (Interface)
Only if the methods are static
Only if cast to Object
questions.explanation: The compiler checks method validity against the reference type. If `method()` is not declared in the interface, `interfaceRef.method()` fails compilation.

questions.question: If class `C` implements interface `I`, what is the relationship between `C` and `I`?
options: `C` is a subtype of `I` (polymorphism holds: `I obj = new C();` is valid)
`C` has no type relationship with `I`
`I` becomes a subclass of `C`
Only static members are shared
questions.explanation: `implements` establishes subtyping: an instance of `C` can be assigned to an `I` reference variable.

questions.question: Can an enum implement an interface in Java?
options: No, enums cannot implement interfaces
Yes, enums can implement interfaces and provide implementations for interface methods
Only if the enum has fewer than 5 constants
Only in Java 17+
questions.explanation: Enums in Java cannot extend classes (since they extend `java.lang.Enum`), but they CAN implement one or more interfaces.

questions.question: What is the recommended annotation to place on interface method implementations in the adopting class?
options: @Implements
@Override
@Contract
@InterfaceMethod
questions.explanation: Since Java 6, `@Override` is fully supported and recommended on interface method implementations to catch typo bugs at compile time.

questions.question: Can a class extend another class AND implement an interface with the same method name and signature?
options: Compile error: signature collision
Yes, the inherited concrete method from the superclass can satisfy the interface contract automatically!
Only if both are declared static
Only if the interface method is private
questions.explanation: If a superclass provides a public method that matches the interface signature, that inherited implementation satisfies the interface contract automatically!

interviewQA.question: Can a class satisfy an interface method contract using a method inherited from its superclass without explicitly overriding it?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. If class `Sub` extends `Super` and implements `InterfaceX`, and `Super` already has a `public void execute()` method matching `InterfaceX`'s signature, `Sub` does not need to re-implement `execute()`. The inherited implementation satisfies the interface contract automatically.

interviewQA.question: What happens if a class implements two interfaces that both declare a method with identical signatures but DIFFERENT primitive return types?
interviewQA.answer: A compile-time error occurs. In Java, a method cannot be overloaded based solely on return type. It is impossible for a single class to provide one method body that simultaneously returns `int` and `String` with the same parameter list. The class cannot compile.

interviewQA.question: Why does the compiler prevent reducing method visibility when implementing interface methods?
interviewQA.answer: This enforces the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP). If an interface declares `public void action()`, client code holding an interface reference expects to call `action()` from anywhere. If an implementing class could reduce visibility to `protected` or package-private, invoking it via the public interface reference would break encapsulation and security guarantees.

interviewQA.question: What are the advantages of declaring service components using interface types (e.g., `PaymentService svc = new StripePaymentService()`) in production systems?
interviewQA.answer: It provides loose coupling, simplifies refactoring, and enables easy testing with mocks or stubs. If the team decides to switch from Stripe to Adyen, only the instantiation site (or dependency injection container) changes; hundreds of consuming classes remain completely untouched.

interviewQA.question: Can a final class implement an interface?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. A `final` class cannot be extended, but it can freely implement interfaces to satisfy capability contracts (e.g. `public final class String implements Serializable, Comparable<String>, CharSequence`).

interviewQA.question: What is the difference in invocation cost between `invokevirtual` and `invokeinterface` in the JVM?
interviewQA.answer: `invokevirtual` indexes into a simple vtable at a fixed offset known at class loading. `invokeinterface` traditionally required searching an itable because different classes implement the same interface at different method offsets. Modern HotSpot JVMs optimize `invokeinterface` using Inline Caching (IC) and JIT monomorphic devirtualization, making the runtime performance gap virtually negligible in practice.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I know the exact syntax order: class Name extends SuperClass implements Interface1, Interface2.
I understand why all implementing methods must be declared public.
I know that abstract classes can implement interfaces without implementing all methods.
I know that inherited superclass methods can satisfy interface contracts.
I understand the collision error when two implemented interfaces have identical signatures but different return types.
I know how to use @Override on interface method implementations.
I understand how the compiler restricts method calls to the reference type.
I understand the Liskov Substitution Principle as it applies to interface implementation.
I can design a domain model combining single class inheritance with multiple interface capabilities.
I know that final classes can implement interfaces.

practiceProblems.title: Warmup: Smart Appliance Implementation
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Complete the `SmartDevice` interface implementation:
1. Interface `SmartDevice`: declares `void connectWifi(String ssid);` and `void disconnect();`.
2. Class `SmartBulb` implementing `SmartDevice`: has `private String bulbId;`.
   - Constructor initializes `bulbId`.
   - `connectWifi(String ssid)` prints `bulbId + ' connected to SSID: ' + ssid`.
   - `disconnect()` prints `bulbId + ' disconnected from WiFi'`.
In `main`, create a `SmartBulb("BULB-01")` as a `SmartDevice` reference, call `connectWifi("HomeNet_5G")`, and call `disconnect()`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
BULB-01 connected to SSID: HomeNet_5G
BULB-01 disconnected from WiFi
hints: In SmartBulb, both methods must be declared public: public void connectWifi(String ssid)

practiceProblems.title: Inherited Class with Auditable Capability
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a financial instrument combining class inheritance and interface implementation from scratch:
1. Base class `FinancialAsset`: has `protected String ticker` and `protected double marketValue`. Constructor initializes both. Method `public void displayAsset()` prints `'Asset: ' + ticker + ' | Value: $' + String.format("%.2f", marketValue)`.
2. Interface `Auditable`: declares `void conductAudit(String auditorName);`.
3. Class `StockHolding` extending `FinancialAsset` and implementing `Auditable`:
   - Constructor accepts `(String ticker, double marketValue)` and calls `super(ticker, marketValue)`.
   - Overrides `conductAudit(String auditorName)` printing `'[AUDIT BY ' + auditorName + '] Verified ticker ' + ticker + ' at $' + String.format("%.2f", marketValue)`.
4. In `Main`, create a `StockHolding("AAPL", 182.50)`. Call `displayAsset()` and `conductAudit("KPMG")`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Asset: AAPL | Value: $182.50
[AUDIT BY KPMG] Verified ticker AAPL at $182.50
hints: Class declaration: class StockHolding extends FinancialAsset implements Auditable
StockHolding inherits displayAsset() and implements conductAudit(String).

practiceProblems.title: Abstract Intermediate Class with Partial Interface Implementation
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Design a partial interface implementation hierarchy from scratch:
1. Interface `DatabaseDriver`: declares `void open();`, `void ping();`, `void close();`.
2. Abstract class `AbstractDriver` implementing `DatabaseDriver`:
   - Has `protected String host`.
   - Constructor sets `host`.
   - Implements `ping()`: prints `'Pinging host: ' + host`.
   - Leaves `open()` and `close()` abstract for subclasses.
3. Concrete class `OracleDriver` extending `AbstractDriver`:
   - Constructor accepts `String host` and calls `super(host)`.
   - Overrides `open()` printing `'Oracle TNS listener opened at ' + host`.
   - Overrides `close()` printing `'Oracle session closed'`.
4. In `Main`, create `DatabaseDriver driver = new OracleDriver("db.corp.net")`. Call `open()`, `ping()`, and `close()`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Oracle TNS listener opened at db.corp.net
Pinging host: db.corp.net
Oracle session closed
hints: AbstractDriver implements DatabaseDriver and implements ping().

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Illegal Keyword Order and Non-public Overrides
practiceProblems.problemStatement: A developer tried to define a `SportsCar` extending `Vehicle` and implementing `TrackMode`, but swapped the order of `extends` and `implements` and forgot the `public` modifier on the overridden method. Fix both compilation errors.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Engine roaring
Twin-turbo boost engaged at 1.8 bar!
hints: Change class SportsCar implements TrackMode extends Vehicle to class SportsCar extends Vehicle implements TrackMode.
Add public to public void activateTurbo().

practiceProblems.title: Polymorphic Notification Sender Queue
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a polymorphic notification dispatcher from scratch:
1. Interface `MessageSender`: declares `boolean send(String recipient, String message);`.
2. Class `EmailSender` implementing `MessageSender`: overrides `send` printing `'[Email] Sent to ' + recipient + ': ' + message` and returns true.
3. Class `SmsSender` implementing `MessageSender`: overrides `send`: if recipient starts with `'+'` prints `'[SMS] Dispatched to ' + recipient + ': ' + message` and returns true; else prints `'[SMS] Error: Invalid international number ' + recipient` and returns false.
4. Class `NotificationQueue`: has method `public void processAll(MessageSender[] senders, String[] recipients, String msg)`:
   - Loops through senders, sending `msg` to `recipients[i]`.
5. In `Main`, test with `EmailSender` and `SmsSender`, recipients `"dev@corp.com"` and `"+15550199"`, and message `'Deploy completed'`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
[Email] Sent to dev@corp.com: Deploy completed
[SMS] Dispatched to +15550199: Deploy completed
hints: NotificationQueue loops over senders and delegates to senders[i].send(...).
